questions.text: Sieverts' law states that the solubility of a diatomic gas in a metal is proportional to:

options.label: b
options.text: The square of its partial pressure

options.label: c
options.text: Its partial pressure to the power $-1$

options.label: d
options.text: The square root of its partial pressure

questions.detailed: Diatomic gases dissolve by dissociating into atoms: $\tfrac12 H_2\rightleftharpoons H\text{(dissolved)}$. The equilibrium then gives $\text{solubility}\propto\sqrt{p_{H_2}}$. This is Sieverts' (square-root) law.

questions.text: The physical reason for the square-root dependence in Sieverts' law is that:

options.label: b
options.text: The gas molecule dissociates into two atoms before dissolving

questions.detailed: A diatomic molecule (H₂, N₂, O₂) must break into two atoms to enter the metal lattice. The atomic concentration therefore scales as $\sqrt{p}$. For a monatomic gas the dependence would be linear.

questions.text: If the partial pressure of hydrogen over a metal is quadrupled, its dissolved hydrogen content becomes:
questions.detailed: Sieverts' law: $C\propto\sqrt{p}$. Quadrupling $p$ multiplies $C$ by $\sqrt{4}=2$. This square-root behaviour is a hallmark of diatomic gas solubility.

questions.text: The equilibrium constant for the dissolution $\tfrac12 H_2(g)\rightleftharpoons H\text{(in metal)}$ is written as:
questions.detailed: $K=\dfrac{[H]}{\sqrt{p_{H_2}}}$ (activities implied). Rearranged, $[H]=K\sqrt{p_{H_2}}$ — Sieverts' law. $K$ itself depends on temperature.

questions.text: The van't Hoff equation describing the temperature dependence of an equilibrium constant is:
questions.detailed: $\dfrac{d\ln K}{dT}=\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2}$. Integrally, $\ln\dfrac{K_2}{K_1}=\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1}-\dfrac1{T_2}\right)$. For exothermic dissolution ($\Delta H<0$), $K$ falls with temperature.

questions.text: At $1000\ \mathrm{K}$, a reaction has $\Delta G^\circ=-20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The equilibrium constant is about:
questions.detailed: $\ln K=-\dfrac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT}=\dfrac{20{,}000}{8.314\times1000}=2.406$, so $K=e^{2.406}\approx11$. A negative $\Delta G^\circ$ gives $K>1$, favouring products.

questions.text: A gas dissolves exothermically in a metal $(\Delta H^\circ<0)$. As temperature increases, its solubility:
questions.detailed: For an exothermic dissolution, raising $T$ reduces $K$ (Le Chatelier: heat is a product), so dissolved gas content falls with temperature. Conversely, endothermic dissolutions (e.g. many gases in liquid metals) show increasing solubility with $T$.

questions.text: Using Sieverts' law $C=k\sqrt{p}$, if at $p_1=0.25\ \mathrm{atm}$ the content is $10\ \mathrm{ppm}$, the content at $p_2=1\ \mathrm{atm}$ is:
Which statements about dissolved gases in metals are correct?

statements.text: Hydrogen solubility in many metals follows $\sqrt{p_{H_2}}$.
The temperature dependence of the Sieverts constant follows a van't Hoff-type relation.
Dissolved gases can embrittle metals (e.g. hydrogen embrittlement).

questions.detailed: All three are true: square-root law (I), $K(T)$ follows van't Hoff (II), and dissolved H/N/O causes embrittlement and defects in metals (III) — the practical reason gas solubility matters so much.

questions.text: Which statement about $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K$ is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: A large positive $K$ corresponds to a positive $\Delta G^\circ$

options.label: b
options.text: A large positive $K$ corresponds to a large negative $\Delta G^\circ$

options.label: d
options.text: $\Delta G^\circ$ and $K$ have the same sign

questions.detailed: $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K$: if $K\gg1$ then $\ln K>0$, so $\Delta G^\circ<0$ — products strongly favoured. As $T$ changes, $K$ shifts according to van't Hoff.

questions.text: For a dissolution reaction with $\Delta H^\circ=+40\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, increasing temperature from $500\ \mathrm{K}$ to $1000\ \mathrm{K}$:
questions.detailed: Endothermic ($\Delta H^\circ>0$) means $d\ln K/dT>0$, so $K$ rises with temperature. Using $\ln(K_2/K_1)=\frac{\Delta H}{R}(1/T_1-1/T_2)=\frac{40000}{8.314}(0.002-0.001)=4.81$, so $K_2/K_1\approx123$ — a big increase.

questions.text: "For a monatomic gas dissolving without dissociation, the solubility would be directly proportional to its partial pressure."
questions.detailed: True. Without dissociation there is no square-root step, so $C\propto p$ (Henry's-law-like linear behaviour). The $\sqrt{p}$ form of Sieverts' law specifically arises from diatomic dissociation.
